I am 51 years old and have farmed these lands in Quzhou County since I was a young man. I never went to school, but I know this soil and this climate with my hands and my eyes. Every year I follow what the village has always done: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plots. It is the safest choice because the grain merchants come to the village, the prices are steady, and I understand these two crops completely. I have ten mu of good flat land.

This autumn I will sow winter wheat again. I still keep seeds from last year’s improved variety — the yield is reliable and I do not have to spend cash on seed. Before sowing I will run the rotary tiller to break up the wheat stubble and level the field. I will put down compound fertilizer as the base and top-dress with urea two or three times when the wheat starts to green up and at jointing. I will irrigate four times: once after sowing to help germination, once before winter to protect the roots from freezing, once at jointing when the stems shoot up, and once during grain filling so the kernels are plump. For pests and weeds I will spray herbicide once and fungicide two or three times — the damp spring air always brings some rust or powdery mildew.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize. For maize I always buy hybrid seed from the market. Hybrids cost more, but they grow fast and strong, and I need the crop to finish before autumn. I will sow directly into the wheat stubble without deep tillage — there is not enough time between harvests, and the no-till machines work fine. Maize needs less water than wheat, so I will irrigate twice: once right after sowing to ensure emergence, and once at the big-trumpet stage when the ears are forming. I will spray herbicide once and insecticide three or four times; the summer heat brings corn borers and armyworms every year.

I thought about planting cotton on two or three mu, because cotton prices were decent a few years ago, but cotton needs more hand labor and more pesticides than I want to manage at my age. I will stick to the wheat-maize rotation on all ten mu. It gives me two harvests a year, the machinery services are cheap because every household does the same crops, and I can sell both grains at the village collection point without bargaining in town.
